data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The covering principle is that the nocturnal UHI is controlled by the ratio of thermal admittance to effective emissivity, where dense urban geometry lowers the effective emissivity of the canyon by trapping longwave radiation, and the cross-city gap scales with the product of thermal mass and building height.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If effective emissivity in canyons is measured to be near unity due to multiple reflections, the emissivity reduction mechanism is negligible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If cities with low thermal admittance (e.g., lightweight construction) but high density still show strong nocturnal UHI, the product of mass and height is not the correct scaling.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speed variations dominate over radiative trapping in observed cooling rates, the effective emissivity principle is secondary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The energy balance at night is governed by the competition between heat release from storage and longwave radiative loss. Urban street canyons with tall buildings reduce the effective sky view, lowering the effective emissivity of the urban surface to the sky. The cooling rate is thus proportional to the thermal admittance (square root of conductivity times heat capacity) divided by the effective emissivity. Cities with greater built density (taller buildings, more mass) have both higher thermal storage and lower effective emissivity, compounding the effect and producing a larger nocturnal gap.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
